lessons.title: Why clean water matters and how to check it
lessons.html:
Water on the farm

Water is used for drinking, for animals, for crops, for spraying and for washing produce. Dirty water can make people and animals sick. It can block drippers and spread plant disease. It can also make sprays work badly.

Where water comes from

  • Boreholes
  • Rivers and streams
  • Farm dams
  • Rainwater tanks
  • Municipal pipes

Each source can become dirty in different ways. A dam can get mud, dead animals or algae. A river can carry waste from upstream. A tank can collect leaves and bird droppings.

Simple checks you can do

You do not need a laboratory for basic checks. Use your eyes and nose every day:

  • Look: Is the water clear, or muddy, green or brown?
  • Smell: Does it smell bad, like rotten eggs or sewage?
  • Surface: Is there oil, foam, scum or dead fish?
  • Around the water: Is there a dead animal, rubbish or a broken pipe nearby?
  • Animals: Are the cattle refusing to drink?

What to do if water looks bad

  1. Do not drink it and do not give it to animals.
  2. Tell your supervisor straight away.
  3. Write down the place, the date and what you saw.
  4. Keep people and animals away if the supervisor tells you to.

Your supervisor may send a water sample to be tested. Testing shows things you cannot see, such as germs or chemicals. Only drink water that the farm says is safe for drinking.

Safety

Never wash spray tanks or chemical containers in a river or dam. Never let chemicals or diesel run into water. Dams can be deep and slippery, so do not swim in them or work alone at the edge.

lessons.title: Keeping water clean every day
lessons.html:
Daily care of water points

Good water quality is not only about checking. It is about stopping dirt from getting into the water in the first place.

Water troughs

  • Clean troughs often. Scrub off green slime and scoop out leaves, dung and dead birds.
  • Check the ball valve so the trough does not overflow and make mud.
  • Keep the ground around the trough firm so animals do not stand in mud.
  • Fix leaks quickly and report broken parts.

Tanks and reservoirs

  • Keep lids closed so animals, birds and dust stay out.
  • Clear the gutters that feed rainwater tanks.
  • Report cracks or rust holes.

Dams and rivers

  • Keep animals from trampling the banks, where possible. Use fenced drinking points.
  • Do not dump rubbish, oil or old chemicals near water.
  • Keep a strip of grass and plants next to rivers. It catches soil before it washes in.

Boreholes

  • Keep the area around the borehole clean and closed.
  • Do not mix chemicals or keep the toilet near the borehole.

Water for washing produce and for spraying

Water that touches food, such as water for washing vegetables, must be clean. Use only the water source the farm has approved. Spray water should be clear, because mud can stop some chemicals from working.

Recording

Many farms keep a simple water record. You may need to write down when you cleaned a trough, what you saw at the dam, or the reading on a water meter. Write clearly and give the record to your supervisor.

Key points

  • Check water every day by looking and smelling.
  • Report bad water at once and keep people and animals away from it.
  • Clean troughs and keep tank lids closed.
  • Never let chemicals, diesel or rubbish get into water.
  • Only drink water the farm says is safe.

To stop the water meter working
